items: A computer is an information processing system which takes instructions from a program
Virtually all electronic devices either are computers or contain them.
Smartphones and tablets are handheld computers.
Many everyday machines, such as airplanes, cars, and electronic musical instruments, contain computers

segments.text: Charles Babbage designed the difference engine, an early mechanical computer, in the 19th Century
Babbage and his daughter, Ada Lovelace, were important figures in the early development of computers.
Below is a picture of an early mechanical computer.

segments.alt: Charles Babbage's Difference Engine on display in a museum case.

lecture_blocks.title: Alan Turing and the Turing Machine

segments.text: British mathematician Alan Turing (1912-1954) developed many of the ideas that led to the development of the modern computer

One of his main conceptions was the Turing Machine, which consisted of a “head” which reads and writes symbols from/to the tape, which moves backwards and forwards so that different parts of the tape. Turing proved that the Turing Machine could execute a very wide range of programs.
Turing influenced John Von Neumann, one of the leading early computer designers.
Turing had a tragic life because he was treated horribly by the British government because he was gay, despite his invaluable services in code-cracking during WWII
Below is a model of a Turing Machine:

segments.alt: A physical model of a Turing Machine with two tape reels.

lecture_blocks.title: ENIAC: The First Electronic Digital Computer

items: ENIAC was designed at the University of Pennsylvania for the US Army in 1945
Used to calculate artillery trajectories and in nuclear weapons research
Made out of 18,000 vacuum tubes (current computers use miniaturized transistors)
Modern day iPhones, iPads, and computers are more than a million times more powerful than ENIAC
Below is a photo of ENIAC.

segments.alt: A preserved section of the ENIAC computer on display at the University of Pennsylvania.

items: The 1970s saw the development of smaller, less expensive computers called minicomputers
This included Digital Equipment Corporation’s PDP-11 and Data General’s Eclipse MV
They were still too expensive for most individuals to own, but became affordable for smaller businesses and schools that couldn’t afford mainframe computers
Tracy Kidder’s The Soul of a New Machine is a good book about the minicomputer era

items: The late 1970s saw the development of the personal computer, which was based on a CPU on a single chip
Best known examples were the IBM PC and its clones, and the Apple Macintosh
PCs and clones ran Microsoft’s MS-DOS and then Microsoft Windows

lecture_blocks.title: 1960s to today: Development of the Internet

items: The Internet grew out of ARPAnet, a US military-sponsored project to connect laboratories, many at universities, that were conducting military-sponsored research
Early applications of the Internet were email and file transfer (FTP)
The World Wide Web was a later application run on the Internet
The following picture shows a timeline of the Internet.

lecture_blocks.title: 1990s: The Development of the World Wide Web

items: In 1989, Tim Berners-Lee and Robert Cailliau invented the World Wide Web at CERN, a physics research laboratory in Switzerland. It was made public in 1991.
Uses the hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP) and hypertext markup language (HTML) to link “pages” and “sites” on different machines on the internet
Early web browser: Netscape Navigator
Grew explosively, requiring the development of web search engines
Google founded in 1998

segments.text: Market power is based on the fact that a network gets more useful and economical the more people participate in it. For instance, if everyone on my block is constantly ordering packages from Amazon, it becomes cheaper for Amazon to supply each item on a per-item basis (economies of scale). A social network is more useful to each of its members the more members it has.

lecture_blocks.title: The Processor (Central Processing Unit or CPU)

items: Every computer has at least one processor and most have several processors
The processor acts as the computer’s “brain” and coordinates all its operations.
A processor can perform four distinct operations (typically within one or more nanoseconds):
Receive a new instruction (fetch)
Make sense of this instruction (decode)
Perform the action defined by this instruction (execute)
Store the result of the action (store)

segments.text: A processor is made up of miniaturized transistors and other components and circuits on a semiconductor “chip.” The following shows a microprocessor chip next to a penny.

segments.alt: An Intel microprocessor next to a United States penny for scale.

items: Advances in microchip design have facilitated the development of computer technology thanks to Moore’s Law. Gordon Moore, one of the founders of Intel, first formulated the law.
Moore’s Law is the empirical observation that the complexity of an integrated circuit (microchip) doubles about every two years.
It’s unclear how much longer Moore’s Law will continue to describe the state of affairs, but it has done so in the past.
Moore’s law is why computers have gotten faster and faster over time.

segments.alt: Our World in Data chart illustrating the growth in transistor counts described by Moore's Law.

items: Computers, like us, need short-term memory in order to function properly
We call this “Random Access Memory” or RAM and it is very fast!
We call it “random” since the computer can selectively read and write to any place in its RAM in a fixed (short) amount of time
When a computer turns off, it loses what is stored in RAM (we call this volatility)
In general, the more RAM a system has, the better it performs. Often the amount of RAM is more important to performance than CPU speed, although that depends on the application.

segments.text: Here's a picture of some RAM "sticks" with memory chips on them.

segments.alt: Three computer RAM modules of different sizes.

items: Temporary storage is accomplished in memory (RAM)
We use RAM for short term memory because it is very fast, but it is also volatile and loses it contents when the computer is shut off
Long term storage is, by definition, non-volatile- it has the ability to persist even if the power is off
It also typically holds far more data than the RAM can
Long term storage devices include hard drives, solid-state drives, and USB “key” drive
Sometimes this storage is available in the cloud

segments.text: The operating system (OS) is:

items: Specialized software that coordinates all activities of the hardware
Used to run all application software through a user interface that starts and stops applications and manages files
Also known as as a “platform” or “software platform”

items: The underlying language, the machine language, of a computer is numerical and is expressed in binary (zeros and ones).
Each code represents an instruction to the CPU (e.g. add two numbers)
High-level languages, like Python and Java, are translated into machine language by a program called an interpreter or a compiler
Python is usually an interpreted language but compilers exist
Compilers produce faster code than interpreters

segments.text: A First Program
The program on the right converts temperature from Fahrenheit to Celsius.

The program uses the input function to get a value of Fahrenheit degrees from the user. It then converts that input to a floating point number using the float function. It stores the result in the degreesF variable. It then converts degreesF to degreesC using a formula, and prints out the result.

code_cells.content:
degreesF=float(input("How many degrees Fahrenheit?"))
degreesC=(degreesF-32)*5/9
print("That is", degreesC,"degrees Celsius")
